paras: The killing of the McKinney family on Kinney Creek was an attack in late May 1881 in which regulators broke into a family's house on Kinney Creek in Carter County, Kentucky, and killed a man and two women named McKinney. It was reported as one of a series of regulator crimes in northeastern Kentucky, and one paper said the family was killed because they refused to be driven from the country. No report gives the victims' first names or race.

The regulators were an organized band active in Carter and neighboring counties, and an Owingsville correspondent wrote that they were operating "more fiercely than ever" even though they were reported to have disbanded. Besides the McKinney killing, the same correspondent listed a house and barn burned for a man named Smith, three men shot and seriously wounded, and several raids in Rowan County near Hogtown. A Cincinnati dispatch said that "almost a reign of terror" ruled in parts of the region.

The McKinney household on the creek consisted of two women and one man, and the Kentucky Gazette of Lexington said the stream took its name from the family. According to the Owingsville correspondent, the regulators visited the family the week before, forced an entrance and killed all three. The Gazette gave a slightly different sequence: the regulators assaulted the house, and "when resistance was offered by the inmates of the house the outlaws fired upon them," killing one man and two women. Only the South Kentuckian of Hopkinsville gave a reason, saying the regulators "murdered" the three "because they refused to be driven from the country."
No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution for the killings appears in the coverage.

The first report was a Cincinnati wire of May 31, which the Omaha Daily Bee printed on June 1 under the heading "Regulator Rule" and the Columbus Journal of Nebraska reworded on June 8. Kentucky papers carried it as state news: the Kentucky Gazette on June 4 called the regulators "self-constituted correctors of the public morals" and "outlaws," and the South Kentuckian on June 7 used the word "murdered." In Ohio, the Eaton Democrat and the Somerset Press both ran the same "Kentucky Regulators" paragraph on June 9, prefaced with the caution "if we can believe an Owingsville correspondent." Every account was brief, none mentioned race, and none followed up on the case.

The accounts differ on how the killing happened: the Owingsville correspondent described the regulators forcing their way in and killing everyone, while the Gazette said they fired only after the family resisted. The creek's name also appears as both "Kinney" and "Kenney."

bases: An organized band of regulators broke into a family's house and killed three people, reportedly for refusing to leave the country, amid a wave of regulator raids, burnings and shootings in Carter and Rowan counties (A1, A3, A5).

Three people were killed by 'regulators', a band the Kentucky Gazette called 'self-constituted correctors of the public morals' and 'outlaws', acting without legal authority (A2, A3, A5); no report gives the band's size, though the plural 'regulators' and the reported organization make a group likely.

A Cincinnati wire, a Lexington weekly and an Owingsville correspondent each report regulators killing a man and two women named McKinney in Carter County, with differing details that suggest separate sources (A1, A2, A5).
